#5144811v2 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms
Docket No. AD26-7-000
 
POST-TECHNICAL CONFERENCE COMMENTS OF 
AMERICAN ELECTRIC POWER COMPANY, INC. 
American Electric Power Company, Inc. (“AEP”) appreciates the opportunity to provide 
these comments to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”) 
following the Commission’s technical conference on governance and stakeholder reforms for PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”). These comments build on AEP’s statement filed in advance of 
the technical conference.1 
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY 
The Commission’s technical conference confirmed Chairman Swett’s conclusion that 
PJM’s “status quo is unacceptable.”2 Commissioner See framed the problem at the outset: “PJM’s 
unique stakeholder process and system of voting” has produced “stalemates”—not “results”—on 
“some of the most consequential questions PJM is grappling with,” causing everyone to “los[e] 
confidence[.]”3 Stakeholders echoed those observations throughout the technical conference and 
in pre-conference filings. 
 
 
1 PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms, Docket No. AD26-7-000, Statement of Stacey Burbure, 
American Electric Power Company, Inc., Panel 1 (filed July 15, 2026) (“AEP Statement”). Unless 
otherwise noted, all materials cited in these comments were submitted in FERC Docket No. AD26-7-000. 
2 FERC, Chairman Laura Swett’s Comments at PJM’s Annual Meeting in Baltimore, MD (May 12, 2026), 
https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/chairman-laura-swetts-comments-pjms-annual-meeting-
baltimore-md-0. 
3 FERC, Commission-Led Technical Conference on PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms at 21:16–
21:38, YOUTUBE (July 23, 2026) (“Technical Conference”) (statement of Comm’r Lindsay See), 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OAGH1c-KENM.

2 
Participants broadly shared AEP’s diagnosis of PJM’s ills. There is broad recognition that 
PJM must act more quickly and decisively. PJM’s governance and stakeholder processes must be 
modernized so that responsibility, authority, and accountability are aligned to produce timely, 
technically sound decisions that maintain reliability, support affordability, and accelerate 
infrastructure development. The PJM governance process must enable economic growth, and most 
importantly, bring new generation online quickly to meet the generational opportunity before us.4 
There is also a near-universal understanding that reform must reconcile the genuine tension 
between Board independence and meaningful stakeholder and state participation. And there is 
widespread agreement that PJM and the Commission should pursue concrete reforms that solve 
identifiable problems rather than focusing on process for process’s sake. 
AEP’s overarching position is results-driven: Ensuring PJM customers are served reliably 
and affordably; developing generation and transmission according to customer-driven timelines; 
and supporting PJM’s ability to evaluate integrated solutions without procedural paralysis. As 
Deputy Secretary of Energy James Danly put it, the “number one priority” in governance reform 
must be “fix[ing] the problems that are inhibiting . . . getting as much supply online as quickly as 
possible, and doing so while protecting ratepayers.”5 Confronting these reliability, affordability, 
resource adequacy, and infrastructure-development challenges requires faster and more integrated 
decision-making. The current governance model was not designed for the speed, complexity, or 
scale of today’s load growth, generation and transmission development needs, and market-design 
challenges. 
 
 
4 See, e.g., AEP Statement at 3-4. 
5 Technical Conference at 46:09–46:26 (statement of Dep. Sec’y of Energy James Danly).

3 
The record also strongly supports AEP’s proposed solutions. First, the stakeholder process 
must be realigned to an advisory model that has the right people at the table, including the states, 
and can provide actionable support to the Board in fulfilling its role. Second, the Board must be 
functionally independent and capable of leading nimbly on the most difficult issues facing the 
region. 
These comments proceed in four parts: 
Part I explains why these governance reforms are inseparable from PJM’s most urgent 
substantive challenge: getting generation online in time to serve new load. 
Part II highlights how the record from the July 23, 2026, technical conference confirms 
the need for governance reform in PJM. 
Part III discusses how to provide PJM’s Board and management clear authority and 
accountability through a true advisory stakeholder model and a reexamination of Federal 
Power Act (“FPA”) Section 205 filing rights over core functional matters.  
Part IV addresses reforms to allow greater state involvement, highlighting the need to 
align filing rights with legal responsibilities while preserving FERC’s role and the rights 
of transmission owners. AEP specifically recommends that PJM adopt a limited, collective 
state filing mechanism for resource adequacy issues and consider a “jump-ball” 
framework. 
Finally, the appendix to these comments responds to the specific questions the Commission posed 
in its July 30, 2026, notice requesting post-conference comments.  
Taken together, the AEP recommendations will modernize PJM’s governance so that 
responsibility, authority, and accountability are aligned to produce timely, technically sound 
decisions that allow PJM to address this century’s most critical challenges.

4 
COMMENTS 
I. 
PJM Must Swiftly Implement Solutions to Help Address Its Most Significant 
Challenge: Getting Generation Online in Time to Meet New Load 
PJM’s most urgent challenge is getting needed generation online quickly enough to meet 
rapidly growing load. But PJM cannot solve that problem if integrated solutions are forced through 
a governance structure that divides responsibility across fragmented committees and distinct filing 
authorities. The same governance defects that prevent PJM from evaluating integrated proposals 
like AEP’s Accelerated Load, Infrastructure, Generation and Network Planning (“ALIGN”) 
concept also prevent PJM from implementing solutions to get generation online promptly. Indeed, 
the persistent governance problems in PJM directly contribute to its current resource adequacy 
challenges: while the region has long seen the current problems coming, potential solutions 
languished for years in deadlocked stakeholder processes. Governance reform thus is not separate 
from generator interconnection or resource adequacy concerns; it is the mechanism needed to 
move necessary reforms from concept to implemented solution. 
The relevant measure of reform should be whether it helps new resources reach commercial 
operation in time to serve customer demand—not whether PJM has merely improved on certain 
governance, queue administration, or study throughput metrics. PJM’s current committee structure 
can take an integrated generation solution and divide it into separate pieces—separating out 
generator interconnection, load interconnection, transmission planning, market design, 
deliverability, and cost allocation—before PJM, stakeholders, or the Board can evaluate whether 
the package solves the underlying reliability problem. That fragmentation does not align with the 
integrated nature of the challenge: generation cannot meet new load unless the project, the network 
upgrades, deliverability, and load-service arrangements are synchronized. A committee-by-

5 
committee process can delay, narrow, or defeat a proposal before the merits of the integrated 
solution are ever considered. 
Commissioner Rosner captured the interdependent nature of the region’s challenges, 
observing that “transmission is needed to interconnect new resources. We can have the fastest 
queue in the world, but if there’s not a grid to plug it in, there’s nothing we can do fast.”6 Divided 
Section 205 filing rights compound the problem. Even if a solution survives stakeholder review, 
implementation may require coordinated changes to the Tariff, Operating Agreement, Reliability 
Assurance Agreement, manuals, and transmission-planning protocols—creating multiple 
procedural gates controlled by different actors with different incentives. The practical consequence 
is delayed generation: when each component of an integrated proposal is subject to separate 
committee review and separate filing authority, PJM cannot reliably move from identifying a need 
to implementing a solution on the timeline necessitated by customers, states, and the system. 
This problem ties directly to AEP’s governance recommendations in these Comments:   
 An advisory stakeholder model would preserve technical input without allowing 
the stakeholder process to become a veto point;  
 Reexamined Section 205 rights would allow reforms related to core functional 
matters to be brought to the Commission efficiently;  
 A more meaningful role for states—with appropriate protections for transmission 
owners’ Section 205 rights—would ensure that decision-making authority within 
PJM aligns with the entities responsible for reliability, affordability, and economic 
development; and  
 
 
6 Technical Conference at 18:43–18:54 (statement of Comm’r David Rosner).

6 
 A more engaged, qualified, and accountable Board would be better situated to 
provide dynamic leadership and ensure timely action.  
Together, these reforms would give PJM the tools to act on the region’s most pressing needs. 
PJM should adopt a near-term action framework that coordinates generator 
interconnection, transmission planning, and load-service review for projects needed to serve new 
demand. That framework should include clear eligibility criteria, synchronized study timelines, 
and Board-level accountability for whether expedited pathways are in fact producing commercial-
operation results. The governance reforms AEP recommends will help achieve this objective. 
Without an advisory process that avoids veto-driven stalemate, clearer filing authority over core 
functional issues, a meaningful and defined role for states, and an informed and accountable 
Board—PJM will continue to identify urgent generation needs faster than it can implement the 
integrated solutions necessary to meet them. 
II. 
The Technical Conference Record Demonstrates the Need for Reform 
The record here demonstrates that stakeholders are broadly aligned in three key areas: First, 
governance reform is necessary to allow PJM to act more efficiently and effectively. Second, 
governance reform must navigate the genuine tension between Board independence and 
stakeholder participation. Third, any governance changes should be solutions-oriented, facilitating 
decisive action to address the region’s most significant challenges rather than focusing on process 
for its own sake. Although there are outer limits to what governance reform alone can accomplish 
to address PJM’s current ills, as Commissioner Chang put it, the simple question on the table is: 
“How can we help PJM make decisions more swiftly?”7 
 
 
7 Technical Conference at 27:37–32:44 (statement of Comm’r Judy Chang) (“[A]s for solutions, PJM 
cannot do this alone. . . . I say this because I want to make clear not every problem at PJM will be fixed 
through changes of the governance structure. And certainly, we will talk about today the stakeholder

7 
A. 
Stakeholders Agree PJM Must Act More Quickly and Decisively 
Everyone, including PJM, agrees that PJM’s current governance system is not delivering 
fast and decisive decision-making. PJM admitted not only that “matters of significance can stall” 
in its stakeholder process, but that its most consequential matters often are the ones that do.8 That 
is in no small part because, as PJM also conceded, the sector-weighted voting structure allows any 
two of five sectors to block action.9 Critical issues that have fallen victim to PJM’s process 
impediments range from resource adequacy and the capacity market to large load integration.10 
PJM, to its credit, did not shy away from recognizing the severe consequences: In this period of 
rapid load growth, these governance failures can “degrade[] reliability, increase[] costs, [and 
reduce] investment certainty in our markets . . . .”11 Preventing such outcomes is PJM’s core 
responsibility, not an optional undertaking. Therefore, PJM’s conclusion that governance reform 
must strengthen its ability to act is table stakes.12 
PJM’s Critical Issue Fast Path process on large load additions illustrates the point. 
Although stakeholders participated “active[ly]” and considered numerous competing reform 
packages, none reached the sector-weighted threshold required for member approval.13 AEP agrees 
 
 
process, decision-making process . . . but these process related challenges even if we can fix it quickly, we 
won’t fix some of the technical and market issues. I want to set the stage and make sure that our expectation 
of change, we set the proper expectations for change.”). 
8 Comments from PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. at 3-6 & tbl. 2 (filed July 16, 2026) (“PJM Comments”). 
9 Id. 
10 Id. at 3-5 & tbl. 2. 
11 Id. at 5. 
12 Id. at 6-7. 
13 Id. at 5-6 & tbl. 4. PJM also highlighted its Reserve Certainty Senior Task Force as another example of 
“the process’s inability to move through a technically complex, yet important issue,” noting that the task 
force currently is targeting a Members Committee vote three years after it was formed, after more than forty 
meetings. Id. at 5.

8 
with PJM that stakeholders receive no trophy for “participation alone,” especially when “timely 
action on matters of significance” is essential to the 60+ million Americans relying on the RTO.14  
State representatives and independent observers reinforced this point. Pat Wood III—
former FERC and Public Utility Commission of Texas Chairman and current Executive Chairman 
of the Hunt Energy Network—called for a “more nimble, transparent process,” recommending that 
PJM transition its stakeholder process to an advisory role and establish direct channels for states 
to bring issues to the Board.15 State representatives from across the PJM footprint—including the 
Organization of PJM States, Inc. (“OPSI”); the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio’s Office of 
the Federal Energy Advocate; Kelsey Bagot of the Virginia State Corporation Commission; Jacob 
Finkel of the Office of the Governor of Pennsylvania (on behalf of the PJM Governors’ 
Collaborative); and Suzanne Jaworowski of the Office of the Governor of Indiana—each 
highlighted PJM’s failure to take timely action on critical issues and supported reforms to improve 
state input, strengthen Board accountability, and enhance PJM’s ability to respond to reliability 
and affordability concerns.16 
 
 
14 Id. at 6. 
15 Recommendations for PJM Governance and Stakeholder Process Reform from Pat Wood III (filed July 
16, 2026) (“Wood Statement”). 
16 See Pre-Conference Comments of the Organization of PJM States, Inc. at 8 (filed July 21, 2026) (“OPSI 
Comments”) (“[F]ar too often the PJM stakeholder process becomes a vehicle for repetition and 
delay . . . .”); Comments of the Public Utilities Commission of Ohio’s Office of the Federal Energy 
Advocate at 6 (filed July 21, 2026) (“Ohio FEA Comments”) (“[S]omething is not working if PJM’s 
stakeholder process is not reaching consensus or able to determine a course of action on pressing issues in 
a timely manner.”); Pre-Conference Comments of Kelsey A. Bagot, Chair, Virginia State Corporation 
Commission at 1 (filed July 21, 2026) (“Bagot Statement”) (arguing “the PJM stakeholder process has 
failed to drive meaningful and timely outcomes for the most critical of issues facing PJM”); Pre-Technical 
Conference Statement of Jacob Finkel, Office of Governor Josh Shapiro, Deputy Secretary of Policy at 10 
(filed July 16, 2026) (“Finkel Statement”) (“[D]urable solutions are impossible without better alignment of 
authority with accountability, which means a more independent Board, a more nimble stakeholder process 
directed at the right type of engagement, and greater involvement from the states in PJM’s decision-making 
processes. Such durable solutions are needed, and needed quickly.”); Written Statement of Suzanne 
Jaworowski, Secretary of Energy and Natural Resources, State of Indiana Office of Governor Mike Braun

9 
Even market participants that resisted major structural change recognized the need for 
faster and more disciplined execution. For instance, Vistra urged PJM to set timelines and 
streamline stakeholder processes, American Municipal Power (“AMP”) called for better issue 
prioritization and workload management, and Constellation identified stronger and more decisive 
PJM leadership as the single most important reform.17 Large load interests agreed that current 
processes fall short, with Google criticizing PJM’s lack of visible leadership during the large-load-
integration process, and the PJM Industrial Customer Coalition calling for better tools to give the 
Board actionable information on time-sensitive issues.18  
Stakeholders disagree on much, but they reached a broad consensus here: PJM’s current 
governance structure fails to facilitate the effective, timely action the region needs, and it must 
change. 
 
 
at 2 (filed July 15, 2026) (“Jaworowski Statement”) (“Sector-weighted voting has value, but the current 
design no longer strikes the right balance between consensus and timely action.”). 
17 See Pre-Conference Statement of J. Arnold Quinn, Senior Vice President, Regulatory Policy, Vistra Corp. 
at 10 (filed July 15, 2026) (“Vistra Statement”) (“Significant streamlining and simplification of the PJM 
stakeholder process would improve both focus and speed. As it stands, the process is needlessly complex, 
time-consuming, and lacks clear objectives or timelines.”); Pre-Technical Conference Statement of Steven 
Lieberman on Behalf of American Municipal Power, Inc. at 2 (filed July 15, 2026) (“AMP Statement”) 
(arguing “the speed of decision-making is largely determined by PJM’s prioritization of issues and meeting 
schedules”); Pre-Conference Statement of Mason Emnett on Behalf of Constellation Energy Generation, 
LLC at 2 (filed July 16, 2026) (“Constellation Statement”) (“When PJM has delayed action, it has been 
because its leadership has decided not to proceed, not because of any lack of authority.”). 
18 See Pre-Filed Statement of Brian D. George on Behalf of Google LLC at 3 (filed July 15, 2026) (“Google 
Statement”) (“It is not unreasonable to posit that with a narrowed and targeted focus, additional efforts to

achieved [on large load additions].”); Pre-Filed Statement of Susan Bruce, Counsel to PJM Industrial 
Customer Coalition at 6 (filed July 15, 2026) (“PJMICC Statement”).

10 
B. 
The Record Reflects a Need to Carefully Calibrate the Board’s and 
Stakeholders’ Roles 
The technical conference confirmed that governance reform must balance two key 
interests: Ensuring PJM is truly independent to achieve its important objectives as an RTO while 
providing a meaningful opportunity for stakeholders and states to participate in PJM decision-
making processes. Several parties—including PJM, OPSI and various other state representatives, 
the PSEG Companies, and Google—called for greater Board authority and independence. They 
offered proposals ranging from expanded or unconditioned Section 205 filing rights for PJM and 
advisory stakeholder voting to revised Board qualifications and reforms to reduce the potential for 
stakeholder stalemates that can block timely filings.19 Others, meanwhile, cautioned against 
reforms that could diminish or limit the stakeholder process. For instance, the PJM Power 
Providers Group, AMP, Constellation, LS Power, Vistra, the Independent Market Monitor, and 
Kent Chandler—R Street Institute fellow and former Kentucky Public Service Commission 
Chairman—generally favored more targeted reforms focused on execution, transparency, state 
engagement, and workflow prioritization rather than wholesale restructuring.20  
As described below, fostering functional independence for PJM and providing stakeholders 
a robust role are not mutually exclusive; they are mutually reinforcing. A well-functioning

Companies at 4 (filed July 15, 2026) (“PSEG Comments”); Google Statement.

(“Chandler Statement”).

11 
stakeholder participation model can deliver timely, transparent, and well-developed input to the 
Board, improving action and outcomes. The stakeholder process, however, cannot endure as a tool 
for a small minority of interests to block progress. This critical moment requires leadership to 
calibrate PJM’s governance structure to advance reforms that balance independence and 
stakeholder participation in a way that promotes engagement and enables solving the pressing 
problems facing the region. 
C. 
Governance Changes Must Emphasize Concrete Reforms, Not Process for 
Process’s Sake 
The record supports focusing on reforms that solve identifiable problems: delay, lack of 
accountability, insufficient state involvement, unclear Board decision-making, and inadequate 
prioritization of urgent issues. PJM itself proposed concrete process improvements, including an 
additional expedited process for high-priority reliability, market, and planning issues; enforceable 
“time gates” for stakeholder processes; conducting more business in writing where appropriate; 
fewer duplicative meetings; clearer issue prioritization; and better use of technology to improve 
transparency and reduce repetition.21 Other participants also offered actionable reform proposals. 
For instance, former FERC Chairman Pat Wood III proposed an advisory stakeholder model, 
binding consultative authority for OPSI, and a complementary state committee, while the PSEG 
Companies proposed Section 205 reforms, changing voting structures or moving to an advisory 
stakeholder process, and Board accountability reviews.22 Other commenters supported enhanced 
state roles paired with greater Board independence;23 firmer Section 205 authority for the Board, 
 
 
21 PJM Comments at 9-10. 
22 See Wood Statement; PSEG Comments at 6-7. 
23 See Finkel Statement; Jaworowski Statement at 1-2.

12 
informed by stakeholder input;24 a funded PJM States Committee modeled on the New England 
States Committee on Electricity (“NESCOE”);25 “jump-ball” filing rights and a dedicated state 
sector;26 or requiring the Board to provide written explanations of its decisions and better 
mechanisms for time-sensitive issues.27 
In weighing these and other proposals, PJM and the Commission should distinguish added 
procedural churn from meaningful governance reform. Additional stakeholder meetings, 
educational sessions, or informal coordination will not be enough to address the serious shortfalls 
in PJM governance practices unless they are paired with results-oriented reforms, such as 
enforceable timelines, clear decision points, defined Board authority, and accountability for 
outcomes. The reforms AEP recommends are designed to meet that standard. 
III. 
PJM’s Board and Management Must Have Clear Authority to Address Reliability, 
Affordability, Resource Adequacy, and Infrastructure Challenges; Stakeholders 
Must Have a Meaningful and Effective Role in Promoting the Best Outcomes 
PJM’s Board and management must be empowered to address the reliability, affordability, 
and resource adequacy challenges confronting the region effectively. To do so, PJM’s governance 
structure must be calibrated to ensure that the Board can lead decisively and nimbly, while 
providing stakeholders a structure for their voices to be heard in a manner that assists the Board in 
achieving the best outcomes. AEP believes that (1) Section 205 filing rights for core functional 
matters should be reallocated; (2) PJM should shift to a purely advisory stakeholder process; and

26 See Overview of Potential Changes to PJM Governance, Delaware Division of the Public Advocate, 
Jameson Tweedie, Public Advocate for Delaware (filed July 20, 2026) (“Tweedie Comments”). 
27 See PJMICC Statement at 5-6.

13 
(3) PJM should adopt other changes that improve the Board’s functionality and its interaction with 
stakeholders.  
A. 
PJM Must Reexamine Section 205 Filing Rights for Core Functional Matters 
PJM’s current division of Section 205 filing rights can impede timely action, particularly 
where an integrated reform requires changes to more than one governing document. In 
apportioning Section 205 rights, PJM and the Commission should distinguish between rights over 
corporate governance of the RTO and rights over core functional matters, such as energy markets, 
regional transmission planning, resource adequacy, and interconnection reform. The Members 
Committee’s Section 205 authority over core functional matters too often operates as a barrier to 
timely and technically sound action.28 Such authority should instead reside with the PJM Board. 
As PJM explained, it holds unconditioned Section 205 rights in some core areas, principally 
the capacity market, but its ability to file changes to the energy and ancillary services markets and 
to the Regional Transmission Expansion Plan process is “conditioned on Members Committee 
approval,” such that, absent such approval, “PJM may be required to proceed under the more 
restrictive requirements of section 206.”29 PJM candidly characterized this division as “in many 
cases[] an accident of history” and noted that its peer RTOs “do not have such conditioning of 
their 205 rights.”30 PJM therefore asked the Commission to consider whether PJM should have 
 
 
28 See PJM Comments at 3-6; AEP Statement, App’x at 7-8. 
29 PJM Comments at 6. 
30 Id. at 7-8. Indeed, it is not clear whether the Commission, in approving PJM’s structure, appreciated the 
effects of this approach. Cf. Bangor Hydro-Electric Co., 96 FERC ¶ 61,063 at 61,259 (2001) (explaining 
that an independent RTO “must have the sole authority to make changes to Market Rules and any other 
changes it deems necessary without being required to seek approval from” a market participant committee); 
N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 96 FERC ¶ 61,059 at 61,186-87 (2001) (rejecting NYISO’s proposal for an 
RTO in which decision-making would be “shared by a non-stakeholder Board of Directors and [a] 
stakeholder Management Committee,” with the Board having the right to make unilateral Section 205 
filings only “in exigent circumstances” because an “RTO must limit the authority of committees of the type 
NYISO employs to an advisory role”).

14 
“unconditioned section 205 filing rights across all its core operational, market and transmission 
planning responsibilities, subject to Board oversight and informed by stakeholder engagement.”31 
The problem is especially acute for provisions addressed in both the Tariff and the 
Operating Agreement. Energy market provisions, for example, appear in substantively identical 
form in both documents, so reform requires approval under both the Board’s and the Members 
Committee’s filing authorities.32 The practical effect is that an integrated solution like AEP’s 
ALIGN concept may require changes to multiple governing documents subject to distinct approval 
requirements33—and too often process defeats substance. AEP therefore supports reforms that 
allow PJM’s Board and management to advance functional reforms efficiently while preserving 
stakeholder input through an advisory process. Consistent with the discussion below, transmission 
owners must retain their appropriate rights and responsibilities under the Consolidated 
Transmission Owners Agreement and related governing documents.34 
B. 
PJM Must Convert the Stakeholder Process Into a True Advisory Model 
PJM should create an advisory stakeholder structure that provides meaningful, actionable 
advice to PJM management and the Board while eliminating the procedural features that too often 
allow stakeholders to block needed reforms. Today, the Members Committee approves actions and 
recommendations by a two-thirds sector-weighted vote.35 Because there are five sectors, any two 
sectors can combine to veto proposals—even where the Board needs timely advice on reliability, 
 
 
31 PJM Comments at 8. 
32 Compare PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff Attach. K-Appendix with PJM Operating Agreement 
Sched. 1. 
33 AEP Statement at 5-6. 
34 See infra Part IV.B. 
35 PJM Operating Agreement § 8.4.

planning, or market-design reforms.36 As AEP’s pre-conference statement explained, the two-
thirds requirement applies not only to amendments to the Operating Agreement, over which the 
Members Committee holds Section 205 filing rights, but also to any recommendation to the 
Board.37 The result is that the Members Committee’s advice “is far too often no advice at all.”38 
Stakeholder engagement remains essential, but stakeholder voting should not dictate 
outcomes when stakeholders are performing an advisory function. Peter Lake, former Senior 
Director of Power on the White House National Energy Dominance Council, made the point 
directly at the technical conference: stakeholders “need a voice in the stakeholder process, but it 
cannot be a veto. We must accelerate gen and load interconnect in PJM.”39 Under a true advisory 
model, stakeholders would retain robust opportunities to offer proposals, test alternatives, identify 
consensus, and create a record for Board consideration. PJM management would develop 
proposals after stakeholder engagement, and the Board would decide whether to proceed—
weighing stakeholder input and accepting accountability for the final decision.40 
Critically, the advisory structure must be flexible enough to allow subject-matter 
committees to evaluate discrete technical issues while also enabling integrated proposals—such as 
AEP’s ALIGN concept—to be considered as a whole rather than being broken up across 
disconnected committees.41 Moving to a purely advisory model would improve PJM’s 
effectiveness and speed in decision-making while strengthening—not diminishing—stakeholder

participation, by focusing on surfacing useful advice and insights and avoiding procedural 
stalemates. This is not a novel construct: The Midcontinent Independent System Operator 
(“MISO”), the Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”), and ISO New England (“ISO-NE”) each employ 
advisory stakeholder processes in which final authority rests with an independent board informed 
by robust stakeholder input.42 
C. 
PJM Must Limit Its Ex Parte Restrictions to Improve Board Transparency, 
Accessibility, and Stakeholder Engagement 
PJM’s broad-ranging challenges—including accelerating load growth, resource adequacy 
concerns, transmission expansion, interconnection reform, and rising expectations from states, 
customers, and federal policymakers—require more frequent and meaningful communication 
between the PJM Board and affected stakeholders. The current rules restricting informal 
communications, however, unnecessarily limit the Board’s ability to understand the real-world 
implications of its governance, market, planning, and reliability decisions. They significantly 
constrain informal engagement between stakeholders and individual Board members outside of 
formal stakeholder proceedings.43 Although safeguards against improper influence are important, 
PJM’s current restrictions are broader than necessary and prevent the Board from hearing directly 
from those most affected by issues of regional significance—including reliability, transmission 
planning, and interconnection reform.  
PJM’s approach is more restrictive than the governance practices of its peer RTOs, and no 
other RTO or ISO imposes such severe restrictions on Board-stakeholder communication.44 
 
 
42 See MISO Transmission Owners Agreement, App’x F (“MISO Bylaws”), Art. VI § 6.1 (Advisory 
Committee); SPP Bylaws §§ 4.1, 5.1; ISO-NE Participants Agreement § 8.1. 
43 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Board of Managers Code of Conduct 3 (rev. Mar. 2026) (“Board Code 
of Conduct”), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-pjm/who-we-are/bom-code.ashx.

ISOs/RTOs, Exeter Assocs., Inc. (Feb. 2021) (“NESCOE Report”) (discussing PJM’s ex parte restrictions

17 
MISO’s corporate-governance framework expressly contemplates that directors may communicate 
with stakeholders, requiring only that a director who receives an unsolicited communication on 
company business report its substance to the CEO and the full Board.45 SPP similarly provides 
stakeholders with substantial opportunities to engage with its Board through open governance 
processes, including Board participation in the work of SPP’s organizational groups.46 These 
examples show that PJM can permit direct stakeholder communication with the Board while 
maintaining transparency, avoiding improper influence, and preserving the integrity of Board 
decision-making. 
The disconnect between the Board and stakeholders created by PJM’s ex parte restrictions 
does not fit the Board’s role. PJM is a public utility, not a regulator; its Board should be an active 
partner in confronting the challenges the region faces, and its policies should not foster the 
misimpression that the Board is providing another layer of regulator-like oversight. Direct 
engagement would help ensure that the Board receives a broad range of practical, operational, 
commercial, and policy perspectives before making decisions that will shape the region’s future. 
Appropriate safeguards can preserve impartiality without insulating the Board from useful 
stakeholder input.47

D. 
PJM Must Implement Additional Targeted Board Reforms to Improve 
Expertise, Engagement, and Accountability 
As detailed in AEP’s pre-conference statement, PJM should adopt several additional, 
targeted Board reforms drawn from the practices of other RTOs and ISOs.49 Without repeating its 
prior comments, AEP reiterates its recommendations of the following reforms to strengthen the 
Board’s ability to address reliability, affordability, resource adequacy, and infrastructure 
challenges swiftly, while preserving the Board’s independence: 
1. PJM should make its President and CEO a voting member of the Board. The 
President and CEO is responsible for implementing Board decisions and managing 
PJM’s operations and therefore should be fully involved in Board decision-making. 
The CEOs of MISO, SPP, and NYISO already serve as voting members of their 
respective boards, subject to appropriate recusal limits.50  
2. PJM Board meetings should be open by default. PJM’s Board meetings are not open 
to the public or stakeholders, leaving very little transparency into how some of the most 
consequential decisions are made. For example, following the Critical Issue Fast Path 
stakeholder process for the reliability backstop procurement, the PJM Board developed 
its own proposal and submitted it to FERC. Stakeholders do not know how the Board 
reached its final decision, what tradeoffs it made, and why certain features were 
selected. AEP strongly supports the Board’s decisive adoption of its own proposal 
following robust stakeholder input. However, future processes should be more 
transparent, which in turn will promote better future engagement and enhance the 
legitimacy of the PJM Board’s decisions. To promote transparency, the Board should 
provide public access to meetings not involving confidential topics (e.g., personnel, 
security).51 
3. PJM should adopt an in-region preference for Board candidates. Given the 
importance of regional knowledge to reliability, affordability, and economic-
development decisions, AEP recommends a preference for Board candidates who 
reside within the PJM footprint or have significant professional experience with the 
region’s electric system. Both ISO-NE and NYISO maintain such preferences.52

4. PJM should shorten its cooling-off period for prospective Board members. Reducing 
the cooling-off period for Board members from two years to one would improve the 
pool of qualified candidates with current industry experience while maintaining Board 
independence. This change would be consistent with MISO’s 2017 reform and with the 
practices of ISO-NE and SPP, which have no cooling-off periods.53  
5. PJM should limit incumbent Board control over nominations. Reducing the role 
incumbent Board members play in the Nominating Committee process would avoid 
status-quo bias and improve accountability to PJM members. CAISO and ERCOT 
provide no formal role for incumbent directors in their nomination processes.54  
These reforms are targeted adjustments, not a wholesale restructuring. Each preserves 
Board independence while improving the Board’s expertise, information flow, accountability, and 
responsiveness—qualities the technical conference record shows the region urgently needs. 
E. 
The Commission Should Not Impose a Novel “Public Interest” Requirement 
Some participants have suggested that PJM’s governing documents be amended to require 
the Board to act in the “public interest.” This proposal, however well intentioned, misconceives 
PJM’s role as an RTO (not a regulator) charged with providing nondiscriminatory open access to 
the regional transmission system, operating the grid reliably, and administering efficient wholesale 
markets that serve customers at least cost.55 A generalized “public interest” obligation would run 
counter to the overriding goal in this proceeding of facilitating nimble and decisive Board action 
by creating an undefined standard that the Board would have to interpret on the front end and that 
could create litigation risk on the back end. Meanwhile, the public interest is already protected—

IV. 
PJM Must Implement Reforms that Allow Greater State Input 
AEP supports targeted reforms to PJM’s governance framework that improve the ability of 
responsible entities to bring concrete, actionable proposals to the Commission under Section 205. 
Any expansion of filing rights should be balanced and carefully defined—preserving the existing 
Section 205 rights of transmission owners while recognizing the central and evolving role of states 
in resource adequacy, affordability, economic development, and public policy matters. The 
Commission should encourage governance reforms that promote timely action, transparency, and 
accountability without undermining the legal responsibilities and investment obligations of 
transmission owners. 
A. 
General Principles: Filing Rights Must Align with Legal Responsibility and 
Reforms Must Enable Timely Action While Preserving FERC’s Role 
Section 205 filing rights should rest with, or be made available to, entities that have direct 
responsibility for serving customers, maintaining reliability, making long-term infrastructure 
investments, and implementing public policy requirements. PJM’s current governance 
framework—including the allocation of Section 205 rights—was developed in a different 
operating environment, one characterized by slower load growth, surplus generation, and 
incremental infrastructure needs.56 As that operating environment has changed, PJM’s governance 
must be updated to align filing authority with legal responsibility regarding today’s reliability, 
resource adequacy, transmission-expansion, and affordability challenges.  
 
 
56 See PJM Comments at 2-3, 7; AEP Statement at 9.

22 
As states bear increasing responsibility for resource adequacy policy, economic 
development strategy, transmission siting, and customer affordability, they should have a defined 
mechanism to advance regional tariff reforms within their collective jurisdiction. OPSI explained 
the point forcefully: state officials “remain accountable for outcomes they have little power to 
formally shape,” and need “a more formal means of presenting their proposals to the Commission 
on a level playing field with PJM and the [transmission owners].”57 At the same time, transmission 
owners must retain meaningful filing rights, because they remain responsible for owning, 
operating, maintaining, and investing in jurisdictional transmission facilities and for complying 
with applicable FERC and reliability obligations. 
Another important reform principle is that PJM’s governance should not require unanimity 
or extended stakeholder deadlock before needed reliability, market, or transmission reforms can 
move forward. Expanding access to Section 205 filing mechanisms can provide a constructive path 
to facilitate innovative solutions while preserving the Commission’s role as the independent 
regulator charged with determining whether a proposal is just and reasonable. As PJM emphasized, 
even where a proposal is filed under Section 205, “stakeholders, of course, may continue to provide 
feedback or challenge the proposal before the Commission,” which “is ultimately responsible for 
determining whether a proposed Tariff change is just and reasonable.”58 A reformed filing-rights 
framework should improve transparency by making disagreements visible to the Commission and 
allowing proposals to be tested in an open record. The ultimate objective should be a governance

authority over many of the solutions).

structure that empowers responsible entities to act, encourages collaboration, and gives the 
Commission a clear record on which to resolve competing proposals. 
B. 
PJM Should Adopt a Limited, Collective State Filing Mechanism for 
Resource Adequacy Issues While Preserving Transmission Owners’ Section 
205 Rights 
AEP supports providing states with a defined and limited ability to initiate Section 205 
filings on matters within their collective jurisdiction—namely, resource adequacy. That authority 
should be exercised through an established regional process, such as OPSI or another collectively 
governed state body, rather than through unilateral filings by individual states. A collective 
mechanism would recognize the important role states play in protecting consumers and advancing 
policy objectives while reducing the risk of fragmented or conflicting individual state filings. 
Several participants advanced complementary versions of this idea. For instance, OPSI proposed 
that, where its members agree on resource adequacy or transmission cost allocation reforms, PJM 
or the transmission owners should be required to provide that solution to FERC “in a way that 
FERC can accept it.”59 And Abraham Silverman, research scholar at Johns Hopkins University 
and principal at SilverGreen Energy Consulting, proposed a funded PJM States Committee, 
modeled on NESCOE, with co-filing rights over at least the resource adequacy portions of the PJM 
Tariff.60  
AEP believes a collective state filing mechanism could provide significant value as PJM 
works to address novel resource adequacy challenges. However, any such collective state filing 
mechanism must be limited to proposals related to resource adequacy issues that are appropriately 
within states’ collective authority, and must not displace or dilute transmission owner filing rights 
 
 
59 OPSI Comments at 1. 
60 Silverman Statement at 2-3.

24 
over transmission rates, planning responsibilities, cost allocation, or the facilities transmission 
owners own and operate. 
Transmission owners must retain their existing Section 205 rights over matters affecting 
transmission rates, revenue requirements, cost allocation, planning responsibilities, transmission 
owner agreements, and the facilities they own and operate.61 These rights are not merely 
procedural; they are essential to enabling transmission owners to fulfill their obligations to 
maintain reliability, invest in the transmission system, comply with FERC and NERC 
requirements, and protect customers. As the Commission made clear in Order No. 2000, “a 
transmission owner must have independent authority to set the level of its portion of the revenue 
requirement to be collected by the RTO.”62 Governance reform must not shift authority away from 
the entities that bear the legal, operational, and financial responsibility for transmission service 
and system performance. Preserving transmission owner filing rights also ensures that the 
Commission receives fully developed alternatives when PJM’s stakeholder processes fail to yield 
timely or adequate reforms. 
C. 
PJM Should Consider a “Jump-Ball” Section 205 Filing Framework 
The Commission should encourage PJM and its stakeholders to consider a “jump-ball” 
filing framework that allows competing Section 205 proposals to be presented to the Commission 
in appropriate circumstances. Such a framework could apply when PJM, the transmission owners, 
or a supermajority of states advance competing proposals on issues implicating their respective 
responsibilities and stakeholder consensus cannot be reached. A jump-ball process follows an 
 
 
61 See PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff § 9.1 (reserving to Transmission Owners the “exclusive and 
unilateral” right to file changes relating to the establishment and recovery of their transmission revenue 
requirements and transmission rate design). 
62 Order No. 2000, FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,089 at 31,076.

25 
established model: ISO-NE’s governing documents already allow a New England Power Pool 
(“NEPOOL”)-supported alternative to be filed alongside the ISO’s own proposal, with the 
Commission free to adopt either proposal that it finds just and reasonable.63 
A jump-ball approach would allow the Commission to evaluate competing just-and-
reasonable proposals in a single proceeding, rather than forcing stakeholders through a more 
burdensome Section 206 complaint process. It would promote efficiency—instead of protracted 
debates at PJM about which specific proposal should be presented to the Commission, multiple 
competing proposals could be developed in parallel. It also would improve accountability and 
encourage negotiation, because parties would know that the Commission may evaluate an 
alternative proposal on the merits. State officials specifically endorsed such a mechanism for 
matters within state jurisdiction.64 Any jump-ball mechanism must include clear eligibility 
standards, voting thresholds, issue limitations, and safeguards to avoid duplicative or strategic 
filings. 
CONCLUSION 
PJM’s stakeholders—from transmission owners and generators to states and consumer 
advocates—are committed to serving customers across the region reliably and at just and 
reasonable rates. But too often, PJM’s governance structure has inhibited, rather than facilitated, 
that essential work. The technical conference record confirms the need for reform and points the 
way toward concrete solutions. PJM should adopt the reforms described above: a true advisory

resource adequacy and transmission cost allocation); Tweedie Comments at 1-2 (proposing that, upon

26 
stakeholder model; a reexamination of Section 205 filing rights over core functional matters; a 
limited, collective state filing mechanism that preserves transmission owners’ rights; consideration 
of a “jump-ball” mechanism; and targeted reforms to improve Board transparency, accessibility, 
expertise, and accountability. These reforms would align legal responsibility, authority, and 
accountability so that PJM can make the timely, technically sound decisions the region urgently 
requires and implement a near-term action framework that will bring generation online in time to 
serve new load.
